executive_summary: NZD/CAD trades at 0.82455, having gained 0.38% over one month, 0.40% over three, 3.38% over six and 4.06% over one year — a pair that has ground relentlessly higher from the 19 November 2025 low of 0.78523 and now sits at the 82nd percentile of its 52-week range, roughly 84 pips beneath the 52-week high of 0.83296. The dominant bilateral narrative is a terms-of-trade scissors that operates in the opposite direction to the rate differential: New Zealand earns a positive and currently widening policy spread over Canada (RBNZ 2.50% versus BoC 2.25%, with +82bp at two years and +114bp at ten), while simultaneously importing every barrel of the refined fuel whose price has risen more than 30% in a month and exporting the dairy whose reference prices have fallen enough to force Fonterra to cut its 2026/27 farmgate forecast from $9.75 to $9.25 per kgMS. Two bilateral differentials diverge sharply from the standalone dossier views. First, Canada's rate problem is entirely a USD problem — against the New Zealand dollar, Canada is the low yielder, so the CAD dossier's Bearish Factor 1 becomes bullish for this pair, an inversion that is easy to miss. Second, both legs carry large speculative shorts (NZD non-commercial −30,027 contracts; CAD leveraged funds −102,495 plus asset managers −101,160), which mutes the pair signal from positioning to near zero and shifts the contrarian edge to whichever short is more extreme — and on a twenty-year percentile basis that is unambiguously the Canadian dollar. Third, and underappreciated, all three central bank decisions inside the strategic horizon fall on identical dates — 2 September, 28 October and 9 December — so this cross has only three genuine relative-policy events and its volatility should cluster on them. We are tactically Bullish with conviction 2 (weighted score +0.1499): the ascending-triangle structure, the bullishly stacked moving averages, the still-repricing RBNZ path and the unpriced 19 August Section 338 tariff on $20bn of Canadian exports all point higher into late August. We are strategically Bearish with conviction 3 (weighted score −0.3097), because at strategic weights the opposing terms of trade, a 3.1-percentage-point current-account gap in Canada's favour, a Fitch Negative outlook on New Zealand against a stable Canadian AAA/Aaa stack, and an 18-month range ceiling that has capped this pair four times all reassert — and because, uniquely among NZD crosses, both standalone strategic dossier views reinforce rather than offset here. The caveat is that carry is irrelevant in this pair (+25bp, a carry-to-vol ratio of 0.037), so neither view is financed by anything other than being right on direction.

market_context.valuation_assessment: The two dossiers disagree materially on pair-level fair value and the disagreement is methodological rather than factual. On the direct REER-ratio method — Canada's BIS REER at 95.71 against New Zealand's at 101.12 (both June 2026) — Canada is 5.35% cheaper in real terms, implying fair value NZD/CAD 0.7813 and marking spot ~5.4% rich. On the deviation-from-own-30-month-mean method used in the NZD dossier, the New Zealand deviation minus the Canadian deviation is +0.08%, implying fair value 0.8261 and marking spot as essentially fair. The reconciliation is that Canada's real rate has fallen further below its own recent history (down 3.4% y/y, lowest print in the retrieved series) while New Zealand's is at the 13th percentile of its own window — both cheap against their own histories, so deviation nets to zero, but Canada's absolute real level is structurally lower, so the ratio method shows the pair rich. Our judgement is the honest fair-value band is 0.78–0.83 and spot at 0.82455 sits in the upper third, a mild strategic headwind. The market has repriced 131bp of RBNZ tightening into the two-year swap while pricing no BoC move until March 2027, implying the differential widens from +25bp to over +100bp — the assumption the strategic view disputes.

market_context.recent_regime: The regime since late June has been a low-volatility grind higher inside a maturing uptrend, driven by relative rate-path repricing rather than by risk appetite. From the 28 June close of 0.80111 the pair added 234 pips in six weeks, with decisive impulses on 9 July (+0.94%, RBNZ hike absorption) and 30 July (+1.16%). The 23 July setback to 0.81203 coincided with a Brent spike toward US$105 and was bought immediately — the pair now treats oil strength as a two-day shock rather than a regime, because CAD has conspicuously failed to monetise it. The dominant narrative has shifted from a near-zero policy differential as recently as April to active divergence in New Zealand's favour.

bilateral_carry_analysis.breakeven_move: At +25bp annualised, a long NZD/CAD position earns approximately 1.6 pips over a 20-trading-day tactical horizon and 10.3 pips over six months; against a 1-standard-deviation four-week move of roughly 155 pips, carry accounts for about 1% of normal variation, so breakeven erasure is not a meaningful constraint in either direction.
bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: The annualised carry (long NZD/CAD) is +25 basis points — RBNZ OCR 2.50% versus BoC target 2.25% — the narrowest positive carry available anywhere in the NZD cross complex. The carry-to-volatility ratio is 0.037 (25bp / 6.8% trailing 60-day realised vol), effectively a zero-carry pair, meaning NZD/CAD is a pure spot expression in both directions: neither long nor short is financed, and holding period must be governed by the catalyst calendar rather than financing cost. Even if the RBNZ hikes to 2.75% while the BoC holds, the differential only doubles to +50bp and the ratio reaches ~0.074 — still negligible. Carry is not working in this pair because there is no carry to work; the pair's six-month advance has been a pure relative-fundamental move, unassisted by financing, which is one reason to take the trend seriously and another reason to expect a quick reversal if fundamentals turn. Forward points show a small discount (CIP-derived, ~+40bp 3-month differential in NZ's favour), and the two-year picture (NZ 3.67% vs Canada 2.85%, +82bp) embeds roughly 1.6% of cumulative NZD/CAD depreciation over two years — the mechanical signature of a currency the market expects to give back its yield in spot, which is the arithmetic basis of the strategic bearish edge.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The differential is +25 basis points in New Zealand's favour and it is the direction of travel, not the level, that matters over four weeks. The RBNZ raised the OCR to 2.50% by consensus on 8 July — the first increase in more than three years — and signalled further increases appear likely; the BoC held at 2.25% on 15 July with its own survey showing no move through December 2026 and a first hike not until March 2027. At the points on the curve where FX actually clears, the NZ advantage is already wider than the policy spread — 2-year +82bp, 10-year +114bp — and both spreads widened through July as NZ's front end priced 131bp of embedded tightening while Canada stayed anchored. The critical bilateral correction is that the Canadian dossier's Bearish Factor 1 is measured against the US dollar, where Canada carries a −137.5bp handicap; against NZD, Canada is the low yielder, so that same Canadian weakness is a bullish input for NZD/CAD. Transmission over four weeks is through the two-year spread, which has no scheduled event to disturb it — neither bank meets before 2 September — so the tactical driver is data-driven repricing: the 13 August RBNZ Survey of Expectations can extend the NZ leg, and Canadian July CPI on 17 August is the only realistic source of a Canadian front-end move, skewed toward a further core undershoot that would widen the gap again.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the differential becomes genuinely two-sided because both legs face repricing risk toward convergence. RBNZ core inflation is anchored at 2.70%, headline 4.1% is an imported energy tax with tradables at 4.9% vs non-tradables 3.4% and falling, and unemployment is forecast to rise to 5.6–5.8% — a central bank with anchored core and a loosening labour market stops at 3.00%, not 3.25–3.50%, trimming the market's 131bp of embedded tightening. On the Canadian side risk runs opposite: the BoC's July MPR assumes WTI stabilising at US$65 against a market at US$84, with a conditional commitment that a sustained oil increase with broadening spillovers would likely require a policy response, and Scotiabank/RBC already forecast hikes to 2.75–3.25%. If RBNZ delivers less than priced and BoC delivers more, the +25bp differential compresses toward zero or inverts — and strikingly, both banks decide on the same three dates (2 September, 28 October, 9 December), so each convergence step is a same-session event. Against that, the level remains positive under almost every plausible path and the 10-year spread of +114bp is not going to invert, so the pair retains small structural yield support even as the priced trajectory deflates.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the clearest example in the pair of two individually bullish standalone views cancelling. New Zealand's data flow is strong: CPI 4.1% beat the RBNZ's expected 3.9% peak, PMI 59.7 (five-year high), ANZ business confidence jumped to 56.1, Q1 GDP +0.8% q/q. Canada's data flow is equally strong: GDP tracking +0.8% q/q in Q2 after 0.0% in Q1, unemployment fell to 6.5% with wages at +3.3%, record retail sales, PMI 53.0. The differentials split by channel: inflation favours the pair rising (+130bp headline, +90bp core), while growth-momentum and labour differentials favour the pair falling (Canada inflecting up, NZ decelerating with a possible Q2 contraction; Canadian unemployment falling, NZ's rising). Canadian releases inside the window outnumber NZ releases three to one, tilting August data-driven variance toward Canada, and Canadian surprises skew positive because its cycle is turning up from a trough. Netting a favourable inflation differential against an unfavourable growth/labour differential, with the release calendar tilted toward the counter-currency, leaves no tactical signal.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the composition of the NZ inflation overshoot becomes decisive and argues against the pair. RBNZ's own projection has headline CPI falling from 4.1% to 3.3% (Q3) to 2.0% by mid-2027 as fuel base effects reverse; core is anchored at 2.7%; two-year inflation expectations are 2.53% and business expectations are falling to 3.14%. Canada's profile runs opposite: the BoC's path embeds Brent near US$75/WTI US$65 against a market ~US$17-19 higher, with war-related cost pressures estimated to peak at +0.4pp in Q1-2027, and business surveys show expectations rising to 3.0-3.5% on oil. The inflation differential narrows from +130bp toward parity or inverts. On growth, Canada projects 0.7% (2026) rising to 1.8% (2027/28) against potential 1.1%/1.3%, closing its output gap; NZ faces unemployment rising to 5.6-5.8% and a contracting housing/residential sector. An economy whose inflation is building and growth accelerating from a trough generates hawkish repricing, while one whose inflation decays and labour loosens generates dovish repricing — both point the pair lower.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: NZD/CAD is a moderate risk-on pair, not a pure one. Both currencies are commodity-linked and both weaken against USD in risk-off episodes; the differential comes from NZD's higher beta (thinnest-liquidity G10 currency, no Fed swap line) against CAD's structurally lower beta (roughly 75% of Canadian goods exports go to the US). Empirically the beta gap is modest: pair realised vol (6.8%) is below either leg's USD pair, as expected from two positively correlated commodity currencies. The current environment is benign (VIX 17.09, IG OAS 0.80%, HY 284bp, NZX 50 at an all-time high) and marginally favours the higher-beta leg — bullish for the pair. But the identity of the current risk driver runs the other way: an energy supply disruption at the Strait of Hormuz is negative for the importer and positive for the exporter, so the risk factor and terms-of-trade factor are the same variable pointing opposite ways for the two legs. The market has absorbed the shock as a term-premium story rather than a risk event, removing classic risk-off transmission but leaving commodity transmission intact. Netting a benign level favouring the base against a hostile driver favouring the quote gives no tactical signal.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the asymmetry of the risk distribution dominates its level, and for this pair the asymmetry is unusually one-sided. Escalation (Hormuz interruption, Brent above US$120) hits NZD twice — risk aversion in the thinnest-liquidity currency with no swap-line backstop, and via the import bill of a country that imports essentially all refined fuel — while lifting CAD's terms of trade. A broad risk-off event (an AI-driven equity correction both banks independently nominate as a principal risk) hurts both against USD but hurts the higher-beta, less-liquid one more. There is no symmetric bullish tail of comparable magnitude: a de-escalation collapsing Brent toward US$70 would help NZ's import bill but also remove the imported inflation driving the RBNZ hiking cycle, partially self-cancelling. That partial self-cancellation on the only bullish tail, against full reinforcement on both bearish tails, is why this factor is directional strategically.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At a 0.20 strategic weight this is the largest single contributor to the strategic view. The mechanism is cumulative balance-of-payments arithmetic. New Zealand runs a current account deficit of 3.95% of GDP against a net international investment liability of 42.8%, requiring continuous foreign capital import, and enters the horizon with a dairy payout cut, a decelerating China (grew 4.3% in Q2, slowest since late 2022, takes ~40% of NZ dairy exports), a rising domestic milk-supply season, and an import bill inflated by a conflict that has left global oil supply 9.4 mb/d below pre-war levels. Canada enters with a current account deficit of only 0.87% of GDP, a record monthly export print of $77.1bn, a bilateral US surplus of $11.6bn, and a REER at 95.71 — the lowest in the retrieved series and 5.35% cheaper than New Zealand's. If oil holds near current levels, Canada accumulates an improving external position while New Zealand deteriorates, and the exchange rate must eventually adjust. Two offsets: Canada's export strength is concentrated (~75% to the US) and ~$20bn faces 50% Section 338 tariffs; and Canadian egress is capped (TMX 85% utilisation, Mainline 95.2%), so Canada monetises price but not volume, selling a discounted heavy barrel with the WTI-WCS spread widened by US$5 to ~US$15. Even after those haircuts the direction is unambiguous and the magnitude is large.

Canadian constraints: egress 85%/95.2% utilisation; WTI-WCS spread widened US$5; ~$20bn exports exposed to 50% Section 338 tariffs
strategic.what_is_priced: The market prices NZ's chronic external deficit as a condition it has learned to ignore and Canada's terms-of-trade windfall as one the currency need not capture — the pair sits 5.4% above its REER-ratio fair value while both legs of the commodity scissors close. The strategic edge has positive convexity for a short: if the conflict persists, Canada's accounts compound in its favour from a decade-cheap real level; if it resolves, oil falls back to a path the pair has already fully discounted.

factors.horizon_split: Stances align and confidence rises four points strategically because the strategic evidence is measured (published current account, NIIP, REER) rather than forecast (two dairy auctions, one trade print). The weight nearly doubles from 0.10 to 0.20 because terms-of-trade effects operate through cumulative balance-of-payments flows: a 31% oil move changes little about export receipts inside four weeks but materially over two quarters.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The guidance differential is genuinely divergent and favours the pair rising over four weeks. The RBNZ delivered its 8 July hike by consensus with no dissent, told the market further OCR increases appear likely, and explicitly named exchange rate depreciation as a channel that could add to medium-term inflation pressures — a de facto asymmetric floor. The BoC's guidance is more ambiguous and net less hawkish at four weeks: Governing Council agreed to look through direct oil effects and reiterate it would not let higher oil prices lead to persistent inflation, even while publishing a conditional trigger for a policy response. The credibility differential between the two is small; both are transparent, high-credibility institutions. The operative bilateral feature is the communication-regime differential: the RBNZ publishes an explicit OCR track (pricing 131bp), the BoC publishes no rate path at all, only projections and assumptions. Over four weeks an explicitly hawkish central bank with no scheduled event to contradict it beats a conditionally hawkish one with the same absence of events, and sequencing amplifies it — RBNZ's next communication (13 August) precedes any Canadian policy signal.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market has priced the RBNZ's words and the BoC's silence. What is not priced is that the RBNZ must publish a marked-to-market OCR track on 2 September for the first time since May, with Brent above US$90 and CPI beating its own forecast — until that track lands the interim drift is hawkish by default.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the guidance differential becomes symmetric and event-dated, with events falling on the same three days: 2 September, 28 October, 9 December. On 2 September the RBNZ publishes an OCR track: a peak at or above 3.50% would validate 131bp and be worth substantial pair upside, while a peak at or below 3.00% removes the front-end support that has carried the base leg. On 28 October the BoC must reconcile a US$65 WTI assumption with an US$84 market against its own published trigger, while facing a Section 338 growth downgrade on the same page — a two-sided Canadian event landing on a day when the RBNZ delivers only a language-based Review. On 9 December both banks report again, after the NZ election and during or just after coalition formation. The credibility differential is the one thing not symmetric: the RBNZ's transparency is its greatest strength and largest single-event risk since a published track can disappoint in a way an unpublished one cannot, while the BoC's credibility is exposed in the softer form of whether it honours a conditional commitment.

strategic.what_is_priced: The market prices RBNZ guidance as credible and directionally hawkish and BoC guidance as passive, treating the 28 October MPR as a non-event. Neither the variance around the NZ track nor the mechanical necessity of the Canadian oil-assumption revision is in the price.

factors.horizon_split: The stance moves from Bullish to Neutral because the tactical window contains only one-sided information — explicit RBNZ hawkishness with nothing scheduled to test it — while the strategic window contains three shared sessions at which both banks' guidance is simultaneously testable, and the tests point in opposite directions. Confidence falls four points because the strategic reading depends on content not yet written.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Raised 0.02 at each horizon. The tactical window contains a dated, unpriced, legally unconditional trade action against the quote currency, and the strategic window contains a dated election with a pre-published rating trigger against the base currency, on top of three shared central bank sessions. Event density in this cross is materially above the G10 norm.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: One dated, unconditional, unpriced adverse event sits inside the tactical window and it is on the quote-currency side. Three presidential proclamations signed 20 July impose Section 338 tariffs of 50% ad valorem on Canadian motor vehicles, alcoholic beverages and dairy — roughly $20bn of trade — effective ~19 August, applying regardless of USMCA origin. This followed the 1 July failure of the USMCA joint review, and Canada has announced no counter-tariffs. New Zealand faces nothing comparable inside four weeks — its binary event, the 7 November election, sits outside the window — so on event risk alone the tactical calendar is one-directional in favour of the pair rising. The market has not discounted it: USD/CAD moved barely a figure across the proclamation week. The offsetting factor is that the Hormuz conflict is a live continuous distribution transmitting adversely to the base currency at every level, via two GDT auctions and the 11 August EIA STEO.

The Hormuz conflict is priced as a bounded oil premium. Both mispricings favour the pair rising over four weeks, but only the first is dated.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the event calendar becomes two-sided in composition and net-negative for the pair. First, New Zealand holds a general election on 7 November, and Fitch has explicitly linked its Negative outlook to it; under MMP, coalition formation routinely takes three to six weeks, extending into December and overlapping the 9 December shared session — converting an ordinary political event into a credit event with a pre-published trigger, with no Canadian analogue (next Canadian election not due until 2029). Second, the Hormuz conflict remains capable of a supply interruption above US$120, bearish through both import-cost and risk channels. Third, and pointing the other way, Section 338 could be extended or the USMCA could terminate — bullish for the pair, the counterweight keeping confidence at 52. Fourth, decelerating Chinese demand (4.3% Q2 growth, slowest since late 2022, ~40% of NZ dairy exports) is base-currency-specific negative. On net, two of four tails point down, one points up, and one (oil de-escalation) is double-edged.

NZ net core Crown debt was 41.3% of GDP with an OBEGALx deficit of 2.6%; Canadian federal debt was 41.2% of GDP with deficits of 2.1% and 1.9%. Functionally identical fiscal positions. The differential is in the ratings stack: NZ carries Moody's Aaa Stable, S&P AA+ Stable and Fitch AA+ Negative (assigned 20 March 2026); Canada carries Aaa/AAA/AAA/AA+, all stable, no action since 2020. Neither market prices any of it — NZ 10yr at +6bp to Treasuries, Canada 10yr the lowest long yield in the commodity G10 — both pricing sovereign risk at zero. No scheduled rating review, budget, auction stress or fiscal announcement on either side inside the window. This factor is dormant for the pair, a deliberate Neutral.

Canada's superior credit is expressed as a lower bond yield, which is precisely what gives New Zealand its +114bp ten-year advantage and therefore supports the pair — fiscal strength in the quote currency is a mechanical positive for the cross through the yield channel.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the fiscal factor becomes directional because one sovereign has a rating agency with a published trigger and an election that determines whether it is pulled, and the other has neither. Fitch revised New Zealand to Negative on 20 March 2026, forecasting general government gross debt rising to 56% of GDP in FY27 from 53.6% in FY25 and a deficit of 4.1% of GDP in FY26; all three stated negative triggers are currently live, including the external one connecting directly to the current account deficit and NIIP. Canada faces no equivalent: its debt path is stable within 41-42%, its borrowing cost sits comfortably below trend growth, and it holds AAA/Aaa from three of four agencies with fiscal space to cushion a trade shock. Transmission is asymmetric: a country funding a 3.95%-of-GDP external deficit expresses a rating shock through its currency rather than its bond market, since its ten-year carries no premium to absorb it, whereas Canada's fiscal position generates no currency channel at all.

expression_assessment.vol_landscape_summary: The volatility landscape cannot be characterised in implied terms for NZD/CAD — no vendor, exchange or retail venue publishes a 1-month or 3-month at-the-money implied volatility, IV percentile, risk reversal or term structure for this cross for mid-2026; realised volatility (~6.8%) sits below both legs' USD pairs.
expression_assessment.directional_expression: Both views should be expressed in spot or forwards, not options. Buying an unpriceable option is not an analytical position. The carry arithmetic reinforces this: at +25bp annualised a long earns 1.6 pips over four weeks and 10.3 over six months while a short pays away the same, so the forward market is effectively free in both directions with no financing reason to prefer a structured expression.
expression_assessment.event_timing_consideration: The three shared central bank dates (2 September, 28 October, 9 December) are the only sessions at which this cross has genuine two-sided event risk, and because no option premium can be observed for them, the correct response is to reduce size into those dates rather than attempt to hedge them — the same conclusion reached for the 7 November election.
expression_assessment.liquidity_note: NZD/CAD is a thin cross executed as two USD legs with wider spreads than either component; sizing rather than stop placement is the correct risk control. The ascending-triangle geometry gives a clean level-based risk framework that partly substitutes for the missing vol surface: a tactical long is invalidated on two consecutive closes below 0.8206 and structurally broken below 0.8144; a strategic short is invalidated on a weekly close above 0.8330. For a lower-beta version of the strategic bearish view, short NZD/NOK remains preferable (175bp of carry, hedges the oil leg), while short NZD/CAD is the better expression for capturing the dairy-versus-oil asymmetry specifically since Norway has no dairy exposure.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Dollar funding conditions are ample and marginally easing, and in a benign funding regime the higher-beta, thinner-liquidity leg outperforms. SOFR fixed at 3.65%, exactly at IORB, with no dislocation across the FOMC date; the Fed's balance sheet stood at $6,738.19bn, up ~$109bn from early March, as QT ended 1 December 2025 and the Desk purchases bills; the broad trade-weighted dollar index depreciated 0.6% m/m; no swap-line drawing reported. Both currencies are USD satellites and most NZD/CAD flow settles through the dollar. The bilateral differential is structural: the RBNZ has no standing Fed swap line; the BoC does, and it is undrawn. In benign conditions that asymmetry is worthless and the higher-beta leg wins; in stressed conditions it is worth several percent against the pair and is currently free. Canada is also the G10's most US-integrated banking system, fast but backstopped, while New Zealand's is slower but unbackstopped. Cross-currency basis for both legs is unobtainable, capping confidence at 46.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market prices ample dollar liquidity as the steady state and charges no premium for the fact that one leg of this cross has a central bank backstop and the other does not. It costs nothing now; it costs a great deal in a squeeze.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the balance-sheet channel dominates the rate channel, and both the direction of the dollar and the asymmetry of the tails favour the quote currency. The Fed has ended runoff and begun purchasing Treasury bills, a structural loosening that has historically weighed on the dollar with a two-to-four-quarter lag. A softer dollar helps both legs but helps the cheaper, better-balanced one more — Canada is 5.35% cheaper on REER, runs a current account deficit of only 0.87% of GDP, and has rising commodity revenue. The dollar-smile geometry is adverse for the base currency at both extremes: dollar exceptionalism hurts the higher-beta, unbackstopped currency; a Hormuz-driven risk-off hurts it and simultaneously explodes its import bill while lifting Canada's export revenue. Only the narrow middle of the smile favours the pair, and staying there for six months requires nothing to happen. New Zealand's 3.95%-of-GDP current account deficit compounds the dependence, with no Fed swap line to backstop its US dollar-borrowing banks.

strategic.what_is_priced: The market prices the end of QT as a technical reserve-management adjustment and charges no funding premium to either currency, including the one with the larger external deficit and no central bank backstop. That is probably right for the central case and wrong in the tails, and for this cross both tails point the same way — negative convexity in a long NZD/CAD position currently free to the seller.

factors.horizon_split: The stance flips because the two channels run on different clocks. The rate channel and current benign funding state transmit within days and favour the higher-beta base currency, giving Bullish tactically. The balance-sheet channel transmits over quarters and favours the cheaper, better-balanced quote currency, giving Bearish strategically. Confidence rises four points into the strategic view despite weaker observability because the argument rests on structural differentials rather than current market state.

tactical.score_interpretation: On the scale used throughout — absolute net score ≤0.10 Neutral, 0.10–0.25 modest directional, 0.25–0.45 clear, 0.45–0.65 strong, 0.65 very strong — a net of +0.1499 is a modest bullish signal for the pair. Five of ten factors are positive, two are negative and three are neutral, and the gross positive of +0.2799 is nearly halved by a gross negative of −0.1300 concentrated in just two factors. Factor 1 alone contributes +0.1440, or 96% of the net score, making this effectively a single-factor tactical call dressed in a ten-factor framework.
tactical.rationale: At the applied tactical weights the pair's direction is set almost entirely by Factor 1 at 0.24, and Factor 1 is the one place where the two standalone dossier views, correctly translated, reinforce rather than conflict. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand has moved from cutting to hiking and told the market that more increases appear likely; the Bank of Canada has told the market nothing will happen for five months and its own survey puts the first hike in March 2027. Because neither bank meets before 2 September, the +25bp policy differential and the +82bp two-year spread are fixed parameters inside the window and cannot disappoint — the only live variable is data-driven repricing, and the New Zealand leg has more of it to do. The critical bilateral correction, and the reason a naive reading of the two dossiers misses this, is that the Canadian dossier's Bearish Factor 1 is measured entirely against the US dollar: against the New Zealand dollar, Canada is the low yielder, so CAD's rate weakness is a bullish input for this cross rather than a bearish one. The weighted score of +0.1499 says this is a modest rather than a robust signal, and the factor interactions explain why: guidance (+0.0392) validates the rate story, the 19 August Section 338 tariff on $20bn of Canadian exports (+0.0385) is a dated, legally unconditional and demonstrably unpriced negative for the quote currency, the ascending-triangle structure with a turned moving-average stack (+0.0260) removes systematic supply, and benign dollar funding (+0.0322) favours the higher-beta leg — but every one of those is a small contribution, and together they only just cover the two genuine negatives. Those negatives are not noise. The terms-of-trade scissors (−0.0640) has both blades closing simultaneously: Brent at US$90.12 after a 20% month is a pure import cost for a country that buys all its refined fuel and a record-revenue event for the world's fourth-largest crude exporter, while GlobalDairyTrade's decline and Fonterra's cut from $9.75 to $9.25 per kgMS strip revenue from the base leg's largest export with no offsetting Canadian effect. And positioning (−0.0660) tips against the pair because, while both legs are short and therefore mute the signal, the Canadian short is at the 99th percentile of a twenty-year series with three dated August catalysts against New Zealand's one. What is priced is the rate story; what is not priced is either blade of the commodity scissors or the Canadian tariff. Over four weeks the path of least resistance is nonetheless higher, toward a further test of 0.8330, because the rate story has no scheduled event to test it while the commodity story needs a specific auction or trade print to be noticed. The dated catalysts are specific and dense: Canadian July labour on 7 August, the EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook on 11 August, the RBNZ Survey of Expectations on 13 August, Canadian July CPI on 17 August, Section 338 effective around 19 August, and Canadian Q2 GDP on 28 August. What makes this more than a coin flip is the coincidence of a policy inflection in the base currency with a dated unpriced trade shock to the quote currency and a technical structure whose failed bearish pattern has already been invalidated — three independent conditions pointing the same way. What keeps conviction at 2 rather than 3 is that four of the six dated catalysts are Canadian and skewed positive for Canada, spot is 84 pips beneath a four-times-rejected ceiling, and the tactical case is one factor deep.
tactical.g10_relative_ranking: Among NZD crosses as a long, NZD/CAD ranks roughly 4th of eight tactically. It sits behind long NZD/CHF (250bp of carry, best carry-to-vol ratio at 0.529), short AUD/NZD (purest relative-policy expression at only 3.93% volatility), and long NZD/JPY (150bp of carry) — all three offering materially more carry than NZD/CAD's +25bp. It beats long NZD/USD (pays 112.5bp against you), long NZD/NOK (175bp against you) and long NZD/SEK. The distinguishing feature is that NZD/CAD is the only long-NZD cross where the counterparty central bank is both lower-yielding and explicitly on hold. Among CAD longs, short NZD/CAD ranks roughly 4th of six tactically, behind long CAD/JPY (+125bp carry plus the cleanest oil asymmetry), short AUD/CAD (widest REER valuation gap in the G10 at 17.44%) and long CAD/CHF (+225bp carry). Across the full non-USD cross opportunity set, tactical long NZD/CAD is a middle-of-the-pack, low-carry, modest-conviction directional expression — roughly 9th-12th of twenty G10 crosses — and is not competitive with higher-carry alternatives unless the specific dairy-versus-oil view is what the position is meant to capture.

risk_reward.asymmetry_assessment: The asymmetry is in the tails, not the base case. A 1.34:1 tail ratio against a 0.45:1 base-to-downside ratio says the modal outcome is a small gain and the distribution is only favourable because the upside tail is a genuine range break while the downside tail stops at a well-defined moving-average cluster. An expected value of +33 pips against a 155-pip 1-standard-deviation move is a thin edge, and that thinness — not any weakness in the individual arguments — is why conviction is 2 and why the position should be sized for a tactical horizon with a defined expiry at 2 September rather than held through it.

strategic.score_interpretation: On the same scale, −0.3097 is a clear bearish signal for the pair — comfortably beyond the ±0.25 threshold and toward the middle of the 'clear' band. Six of ten factors are negative, four are neutral and none is positive, an unusually one-sided distribution reflecting a genuine bilateral fact: strategically the base dossier is Bearish and the quote dossier is Bullish on its own currency, so both standalone views push this cross the same way. Terms of Trade at −0.1360 is 44% of the gross negative and reflects both the raised 0.20 weight and the highest confidence in the report at 68. The two heaviest weights other than Factor 5 — Policy & Rates at 0.24 and Guidance at 0.12, together 36% of the scheme — are both Neutral and contribute nothing.
strategic.rationale: At strategic weights the scheme is dominated by Policy & Rates at 0.24, External Balance and Terms of Trade at 0.20, Guidance at 0.12 and USD Liquidity at 0.08, and the decisive fact is that the first and third of those are Neutral, leaving the terms-of-trade factor to set the direction. Policy & Rates is Neutral rather than Bullish at this horizon on arithmetic rather than judgement: the level of the differential remains positive under every plausible path — even an RBNZ at 3.00% against a BoC at 2.75% leaves +25bp, and the +114bp ten-year spread will not invert — but the priced trajectory assumes the RBNZ delivers all 131bp of embedded tightening while the Bank of Canada does nothing until March 2027, and both legs of that assumption are more likely to be wrong in the pair-negative direction. New Zealand's core inflation is anchored at 2.70% with unemployment heading to 5.6-5.8%, arguing for a 3.00% terminal rather than 3.25-3.50%; Canada's July MPR is built on a US$65 WTI assumption against an US$84 market with a published commitment to respond if oil-driven inflation broadens, and two of three sell-side houses already forecast BoC hikes. A positive level with a deflating trajectory is genuinely two-sided. Strip out the policy story that is already in the price and what remains is the strategic case, and it is one-directional. Terms of trade (−0.1360) is the largest contributor because this is the G10's cleanest commodity-versus-commodity pair and both blades of the scissors are closing: New Zealand exports the dairy whose reference prices forced a farmgate downgrade and imports the fuel that rose more than 20% in a month, while Canada exports that fuel into record volumes and imports dairy under supply management. The interactions reinforce: the terms-of-trade deterioration widens the current account deficit that Fitch has explicitly named as a negative trigger, the energy conflict that drives it is the same variable driving the risk factor and one leg of the event risk, the growth and inflation paths cross in the same direction, and a softening dollar under an expanding Fed balance sheet favours the cheaper, better-balanced leg. Bilateral trade between the two economies is immaterial to all of this — a net balance of $0.2bn — so nothing in the direct relationship offsets the third-market commodity channel. What is priced is a widening New Zealand rate advantage and, on the derived bank cross matrix, a Q4-2026 level of roughly 0.820, essentially spot. What we expect is 0.7950, because the priced rate path deflates while the terms-of-trade and external differentials compound. The path of least resistance is lower once the 2 September shared session removes the repricing catalyst, and the dated catalysts are the three shared central bank sessions, the 7 November New Zealand election with its pre-published Fitch trigger, and the fortnightly dairy auction cadence. What makes this more than a coin flip is that the negative factors rest on measured, published facts while the pair's support rests on a forecast path the market has already fully bought. Conviction is 3 and not 4 because 36% of the scheme is Neutral, because the 0.8000 structural floor and the +25bp differential are genuine brakes, and because a negotiated withdrawal of the Section 338 tariffs would remove a real Canadian discount.

Its ranking would fall sharply on a Hormuz settlement and rise sharply on an escalation.

risk_reward.asymmetry_assessment: The distribution is genuinely and materially positively skewed for a short, and unusually so for a cross this quiet. The favourable tail is 2.66 times the adverse tail at equal probabilities, because the two scenarios that would drive it — a Hormuz closure and a post-election New Zealand rating action — each move both legs in the same direction, whereas the adverse scenario requires the RBNZ to over-deliver and the Bank of Canada to under-deliver simultaneously. That double-reinforcement on the downside against double-conditionality on the upside is why this is the highest-quality risk/reward in either horizon.

consensus_divergence.bank_consensus_forecast: No major bank publishes a standalone NZD/CAD forecast; a derived bank mean of roughly 0.820 (Q4-2026) is constructed by multiplying published NZD/USD and USD/CAD forecasts across six bank pairings, with a dispersion of 0.781 (BNZ×TD) to 0.877 (ANZ×Scotiabank) — a 9.6-figure range that carries almost no information.
consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: Tactically above nearly all published near-term paths (bank derived and algorithmic); strategically below the derived bank mean but above the bearish quantitative/algorithmic models
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: +480 to +570 pips above the nearest algorithmic near-term consensus at the tactical horizon; approximately −250 pips below the derived bank mean at the strategic horizon
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: Three specific reasons. First, the derived bank crosses are arithmetic artefacts, not views — the 9.6-figure dispersion exists because unrelated NZD/USD and USD/CAD forecasts are multiplied without sanity-checking against the cross's own 18-month range, producing implied levels like 0.877 that have never traded in this cycle. Our contribution is to price the cross on its own bilateral differentials rather than as a residual. Second, the quantitative/retail models are extrapolating a trend that has already reversed — they were calibrated on a series that fell from 0.833 to 0.785 in 2025 and their bearish near-term paths are inconsistent with a pair whose moving averages are now bullishly stacked and whose most recent bearish chart pattern failed. Third, and the substantive strategic disagreement, nobody prices the commodity scissors: published forecasts model dairy through NZD/USD and oil through USD/CAD as independent variables when for this cross they are two blades of a single instrument, and that configuration is worth several percent over six months and appears in no published forecast.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: The tactical view captures roughly 480 pips of relative outperformance against the nearest algorithmic near-term path; the strategic view captures roughly 250 pips against the derived bank mean. Expressed as a paired sequence — long into 2 September, then short — the combined move is on the order of 5.0-5.5% before financing, with carry immaterial in both legs.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: The specific way we are wrong on the tactical leg is that Section 338 is deferred in the days before 19 August, removing the pair's cleanest bullish catalyst and validating the models' bearish near-term paths. The specific way we are wrong on the strategic leg is that the Hormuz conflict resolves and Brent returns toward the EIA's US$65 2027 path, removing the import-cost drag on the base currency and the export-revenue support for the quote currency simultaneously, collapsing the terms-of-trade pillar that carries 44% of the strategic gross negative — in that world 0.8450 or higher is realistic, a 2.49% loss on the short.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The mechanism is that the two horizons pay for different things and this pair's differentials are unusually cleanly split between them. At two to four weeks the price is set by the change in expected rate differentials and by dated events, and the factors that express change — Policy & Rates, Guidance, Event Risk and Market Structure, together 0.43 of the tactical scheme — are all positive for the pair. At one to six months the price is set by the level of the differential actually earned and by cumulative balance-of-payments flows, and the factors that express level — External Balance, Fiscal and Event Risk, together 0.34 of the strategic scheme against 0.21 tactically — are all negative, while Policy & Rates goes Neutral. The single most important reweighting is Factor 5, which rises from 0.10 to 0.20 and swings from a −0.0640 contribution to a −0.1360 one: the commodity scissors barely matter over four weeks but dominate over two quarters, the timescale on which current accounts are actually settled. Nine of ten factors carry the same or an adjacent reading at both horizons — the divergence is generated by the reweighting, not by disagreement about the facts.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: 2026-09-02 (first shared RBNZ/Bank of Canada session, at which the RBNZ must publish an explicit OCR track for the first time since May), with 2026-10-28 (the only shared session at which the Bank of Canada publishes an assumption revision while the RBNZ delivers language alone) as a secondary and more decisive inflection.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Run the tactical long into 2 September, then reverse. Practically: hold long NZD/CAD or a long via the spot/forward market through the 19 August tariff date and into late August, reduce into 2 September, and establish the strategic short on the other side of the published OCR track. Do not attempt to hold a single position across the inflection — the factor weights change too much, Factor 5's contribution doubles, and the November election plus coalition formation make the second half of the strategic horizon materially more volatile than the first. Because carry is +25bp and therefore irrelevant in both directions, there is no financing penalty to switching sides.

A reversal in the cores above 2.00% would revive the BoC's hawkish option and compress the +82bp two-year spread, bearish for the pair; a further decline toward 1.70% would foreclose it for 2026 and be bullish. Given the Canadian growth inflection, the risk to the cores is to the upside.

For a non-USD cross the transmission is indirect: a hawkish read pulls the dollar toward the exceptionalism side of the smile, hurting the higher-beta, unbackstopped base leg more than the quote leg, mildly bearish for the pair.

catalysts.rationale: The single most important bilateral event for NZD/CAD, its significance coming from the coincidence of dates. The RBNZ is roughly 70-80% priced to hike to 2.75% and must publish an explicit OCR track for the first time since May; the Bank of Canada is near-certain to hold at 2.25%, with the information in whether it maintains pure look-through framing or leans on its conditional trigger. A track peaking at 3.50% against unqualified Canadian look-through is worth 150-250 pips of pair upside; a track at 3.00% against any Canadian oil acknowledgement is worth 200-300 pips of downside. Because both banks report the same session, the cross prices the differential directly rather than sequentially — why this is the tactical view's expiry date.

The RBNZ has stated that domestic economic activity slowed in the June quarter as the oil shock weighed on demand, with bank forecasts running to a 0.1-0.3% contraction. Landing roughly three weeks after Canada confirms +0.8%, a negative New Zealand print would complete the inversion of the growth-momentum differential inside a single month — the clearest single confirmation of the strategic bear case available in the calendar.

catalysts.event: Statistics New Zealand Q3 2026 Consumer Price Index
catalysts.rationale: The RBNZ projects headline inflation falling from 4.1% to 3.3% as direct fuel effects reverse. A print at or below 3.3% would confirm the overshoot was an imported energy tax rather than a domestic inflation problem, undercutting the market's 131bp terminal and compressing the inflation differential over Canada toward +50bp, precisely as Canadian war-related cost pressures build toward their projected Q1-2027 peak.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada decision and Monetary Policy Report AND RBNZ Monetary Policy Review (same day)
catalysts.rationale: The most asymmetric of the three shared sessions and the strategic view's decisive catalyst. The Bank of Canada's July MPR assumed Brent near US$75 in Q3-2026 settling to US$70, and WTI stabilising at US$65; against WTI at US$84 it must raise its oil path, mechanically lifting near-term inflation and forcing Governing Council to confront its published statement that such a scenario would likely require a policy response. Partially offsetting, the same MPR must cut growth because its 5.0% average-tariff assumption predates Section 338. Crucially, the RBNZ delivers only a Monetary Policy Review that day — no published OCR track — so the base leg has no comparable revision mechanism.

Fitch has explicitly stated that significant New Zealand fiscal consolidation is likely only after this election and that it adds uncertainty to the fiscal outlook. Under mixed-member proportional representation, coalition formation routinely takes three to six weeks, extending uncertainty into December and overlapping the 9 December shared session. The bilateral asymmetry is total: Canada's next federal election is not due until 2029, so the pair carries a one-sided electoral risk premium against its base currency, expressed in the currency because its ten-year at +6bp to Treasuries carries no premium to absorb a rating shock.

catalysts.event: RBNZ Monetary Policy Statement AND Bank of Canada decision (same day)
catalysts.rationale: The third and final shared session inside the strategic horizon, and the point at which both terminal rates become settled questions. It falls after the New Zealand election and during or just after coalition formation, so the RBNZ track will incorporate the fiscal outlook for the first time; it is also the meeting at which any 28 October Canadian oil-assumption revision would translate into action or explicit signalling. We assign roughly 40-45% to a Bank of Canada hike or explicit hawkish signal by this date if WTI holds above US$80.

catalysts.event: Continuous: Brent and WTI front-month price path
catalysts.rationale: The single most important continuous variable for this cross and the one the market is demonstrably not pricing into it. Brent at US$90.12 and WTI at US$84.25, after a 20% and ~31% monthly rise respectively, is simultaneously the largest import cost for the base currency and the largest export revenue for the quote currency — and the pair rose 0.38% over the same month. Every US$1 on the barrel is worth roughly US$1.5bn a year to Canadian export receipts, and roughly a quarter of New Zealand's June-quarter CPI overshoot. There is no scheduled date; the transmission is daily.

invalidators.condition: Brent falls below US$70 per barrel on a durable Strait of Hormuz settlement and holds there for four weeks
invalidators.mechanism: This is the only single event that reverses both blades of the terms-of-trade scissors simultaneously for this specific pair — it removes the import-cost drag on the base currency, removes the export-revenue support for the quote currency, and collapses the −0.1360 strategic contribution from Factor 5 that is 44% of the gross negative. No other variable does all three.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: Brent front-month settlement; IEA-reported Gulf export volumes

invalidators.condition: GlobalDairyTrade rises more than 5% cumulatively across two consecutive auctions with whole milk powder clearing US$3,800/tonne, while WTI simultaneously trades below US$78
invalidators.mechanism: This is the specific joint condition that inverts the pair's commodity netting — dairy re-rating restores the base leg's export revenue and forces a Fonterra upgrade, while sub-US$78 crude removes the quote leg's revenue windfall. Either condition alone is insufficient.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: GDT event results and whole milk powder average winning price against WTI Cushing spot

invalidators.condition: The 2 September RBNZ Monetary Policy Statement publishes an OCR track peaking at 3.50% or above while the Bank of Canada, in the same session, reaffirms 2.25% through 2026 with unqualified look-through language
invalidators.mechanism: The entire strategic bear case rests on the priced +100bp policy differential deflating rather than being validated. A 3.50% NZ terminal against an unmoved BoC takes the differential toward +125bp on the forward path, turns Factor 1 decisively Bullish and Factor 6 with it, lifting the strategic score from −0.3097 to approximately −0.13.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: Published RBNZ OCR track peak; NZ-Canada two-year spread

invalidators.condition: NZD/CAD posts two consecutive weekly closes above 0.83296
invalidators.mechanism: The 18-month range whose upper boundary has rejected price four times is the structural premise on which a 0.7950 mean-reversion target rests. A confirmed break through that boundary would mean the cross has re-rated on a differential we have mis-weighted, opening 0.8450 rather than 0.7950.

invalidators.condition: Canadian leveraged-fund net shorts cover to shallower than −70,000 contracts across two consecutive COT reports without USD/CAD falling
invalidators.mechanism: The pair's principal near-term downside driver is a Canadian squeeze from a twenty-year positioning extreme; voluntary covering into flat spot exhausts that fuel without delivering the move, removing the −0.0660 tactical contribution from Factor 4 and inverting the positioning asymmetry in the pair's favour.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: CFTC Traders in Financial Futures, Canadian dollar, against USD/CAD spot

invalidators.condition: The Section 338 tariffs are extended beyond vehicles, alcohol and dairy to auto parts or lumber, or Canada announces broad counter-tariffs
invalidators.mechanism: The affected Canadian export base moves from roughly $20bn toward a multiple of that, opening a Canada-specific risk premium materially larger than New Zealand's election-plus-Fitch discount can offset, and forcing a growth downgrade on 28 October that would neutralise the hawkish oil revision the strategic case relies on.

invalidators.condition: New Zealand Q2 GDP contracts by more than 0.3% in the mid-September release while Canada has confirmed +0.8% quarterly on 28 August
invalidators.mechanism: The growth-momentum differential would invert by more than 1.1 percentage points inside three weeks, removing the data support beneath the RBNZ hiking narrative carrying the base leg and validating the Bank of Canada's growth-has-resumed framing ahead of the 28 October MPR.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: Statistics New Zealand quarterly GDP against Statistics Canada Q2 income-and-expenditure GDP

signposts.confirms_if: narrows inside +50bp (bearish confirmation, as the RBNZ track disappoints and/or Canadian front end reprices hawkish)
signposts.invalidates_if: widens beyond +110bp for five consecutive sessions
signposts.bilateral_importance: This is the pair's single most direct driver and it is the one spread nobody publishes — the market watches NZ-US and Canada-US separately and never triangulates them, which is precisely why the cross's rate story is under-analysed.

signposts.indicator: Brent crude against GlobalDairyTrade whole milk powder — the terms-of-trade scissors
signposts.current_level: Brent US$90.12 (31 July settle); whole milk powder US$3,486/tonne (23 July auction)
signposts.confirms_if: Brent holds above US$85 while whole milk powder holds below US$3,600 — both blades closing
signposts.invalidates_if: Brent below US$78 and whole milk powder above US$3,800 — both blades reversing
signposts.bilateral_importance: This composite matters more for NZD/CAD than for any other G10 cross, because it is the only pair in which one currency's dominant export is the other currency's negligible import and vice versa.

signposts.indicator: NZD/CAD spot against the 200-day moving average and the 18-month range ceiling
signposts.current_level: 0.82455, above the 50-day (0.81441), 100-day (0.81274) and 200-day (0.81091); 84 pips below the 52-week high of 0.83296
signposts.confirms_if: tactically, spot holds above 0.8206 and tests 0.8330; strategically, spot closes below the 0.8109 200-day after 2 September
signposts.bilateral_importance: Because there is no obtainable implied volatility surface, no risk reversal and no term structure for this cross, level-based structure is the only market-derived read available — it substitutes for the vol surface that exists for every major pair.
signposts.frequency: Daily, with weekly closes for the range test

signposts.indicator: CFTC positioning ratio — Canadian leveraged-fund net short as a share of open interest versus New Zealand non-commercial net short as a share of open interest
signposts.confirms_if: the Canadian ratio deepens relative to the New Zealand ratio, or the Canadian short covers with USD/CAD falling (a genuine squeeze rather than voluntary exit)
signposts.invalidates_if: the Canadian ratio covers shallower than −20% of OI while the New Zealand short holds beyond −28% of OI
signposts.bilateral_importance: For either currency alone the raw contract count is the signal; for the cross only the ratio matters, because two shorts of equal proportional size cancel. Nobody publishes this comparison, and it is the reason the pair's positioning signal is muted rather than bullish despite two extreme shorts.

signposts.indicator: RBNZ published OCR track peak versus Bank of Canada market-implied first-hike date
signposts.current_level: RBNZ track not published since May (next 2 September); 131bp embedded against a 2.50% cash rate. Bank of Canada market-implied first hike March 2027, survey terminal 2.75%
signposts.confirms_if: the 2 September RBNZ track peaks at or below 3.00% and Bank of Canada pricing pulls the first hike into Q4-2026 or January 2027
signposts.invalidates_if: the RBNZ track peaks at or above 3.50% and Bank of Canada pricing remains unchanged at March 2027
signposts.bilateral_importance: A genuinely bilateral indicator with no standalone analogue, unusually clean because both central banks decide on the same three dates. For most crosses relative policy is inferred from sequential meetings; here it is priced in single sessions, concentrating the pair's entire policy variance into three days.
signposts.frequency: Three decision dates in the horizon; swap-implied pricing daily

signposts.indicator: Canada's bilateral merchandise surplus with the United States
signposts.current_level: +$11.6bn (May 2026), up from $10.3bn in April — the largest since January 2025, on record total exports of $77.1bn
signposts.confirms_if: holds above $11.0bn in the June and July prints, demonstrating that higher oil prices are reaching the Canadian current account despite the WCS discount and egress constraints
signposts.invalidates_if: falls below $8.0bn, indicating either that Section 338 is biting faster than expected or that the price gain is being absorbed by the differential
signposts.bilateral_importance: The pair's strategic case rests on Canada's external accounts compounding in its favour while New Zealand's deteriorate, and this is the line item where the oil windfall shows up — not in the trade-weighted index and not in the oil price itself. It also carries the Section 338 signal.

assumptions: The valuation date is 2026-08-01, taken from the base dossier metadata, while the supplied price series runs to 2026-08-06 with a final close of 0.82455. All spot-referenced levels, pip calculations, targets, moving averages, range percentiles and performance figures use the price data as the source of truth, anchored on 0.82455 as of 6 August.

Both dossiers independently quote NZD/CAD at 0.82541 and 0.82540 for 31 July, an 8-9 pip difference from the price series' 31 July close of 0.82521, reflecting different closing conventions; the discrepancy is immaterial and the price series is used throughout.

The 5 August New Zealand Q2 labour market release falls inside the price window but outside the dossier window, so its effect may be partly embedded in nearby closes; we have not attempted to infer its content from price action, and it is excluded from the catalyst list.

Implied volatility, risk reversals and the variance risk premium are unobtainable for this cross and are stated as gaps, not estimated. Rather than manufacture a number, Factor 9's confidence has been set low at both horizons, no variance risk premium or risk-reversal direction is asserted anywhere, and the expression assessment concludes both views must be expressed in spot or forwards.

Realised volatility (20-day 6.4%, ~60-day 6.8%, ~90-day 6.7%) is computed from the supplied OHLC series and is internally consistent but not externally reproducible; all carry-to-volatility ratios divide the annualised policy-rate differential by trailing realised volatility because implied volatility is unobservable.

Forward points are CIP-derived, not quoted; traded NZD/CAD forward points could not be obtained from a public venue. Forwards use an approximate +40bp three-month rate differential with an uncertainty of roughly ±10 basis points, i.e., roughly ±4 pips on the six-month outright.

The pair-level valuation conflict is disclosed rather than resolved: 0.8261 fair value on the deviation-from-own-mean method versus 0.7813 on the direct REER-ratio method. We report both, treat the honest fair-value band as 0.78-0.83, and note no target in this report is derived from either valuation figure.

Bilateral trade is taken directly from the injected IMF DOTS block and was not re-estimated from the web. The directional asymmetry between reporting sides (NZ reports $0.7bn of exports where Canada reports $0.9bn of imports) is a normal consequence of differing valuation and transhipment conventions and does not affect any conclusion.

Commodity netting follows the framework's stated direction rules applied bilaterally; the ±10% scenario magnitudes are order-of-magnitude judgements derived from Canadian export volumes and New Zealand dairy production shares, not modelled elasticities, and the oil scenario is deliberately asymmetric because a lower oil price also erodes the RBNZ hiking case supporting the base leg.

Six factors were adjusted at each horizon, none by more than ±0.04, netting to exactly zero. Factor 5 (up) and Factor 10 (down) are explicitly contemplated by the framework; the reductions to Factors 2 and 3 are pair-specific rather than framework-prescribed, and Factor 9 was left at default despite a structural case because the absence of volatility data means it cannot bear additional weight.

Positioning normalisation uses net contracts as a share of each currency's own total open interest rather than raw contract counts, because New Zealand dollar open interest (105,128) is 28% of Canada's (372,447) and raw counts are not comparable. Both dossiers' positioning data carry their own caveats which propagate here, including an unreconciled alternative New Zealand series reporting −47.7k rather than −30.0k.

The coincidence of RBNZ and Bank of Canada decisions on 2 September, 28 October and 9 December 2026 is stated separately in each dossier's own calendar and is not an inference; it is, in our view, the most consequential structural feature of this cross that neither standalone analysis identifies.

Consensus derivation multiplies published NZD/USD forecasts by published USD/CAD forecasts, both drawn from the two dossiers' consensus sections, which compounds two independent forecast errors and mixes vintages, none of which can incorporate the 20 July Section 338 proclamation. The resulting 9.6-figure dispersion should be read as evidence that no institutional view exists on this cross, not as a distribution of considered opinions.

Support and resistance levels sourced from the web come from retail technical-analysis publishers rather than institutional desks; only levels that coincide with a structure independently visible in the supplied price data, or round numbers with obvious psychological standing, were retained. The 52-week high, 52-week low and all three moving averages come from the price data, not the web.

Scenario probabilities are subjective and follow the framework's standard 50/25/25 base/upside/downside structure at both horizons. Individual invalidator probabilities are our own estimates and do not sum to 100% because the conditions are not mutually exclusive.
